subject: Masotti et al. (2008)
object: Masotti et al. (2008) described a multigeneration family (F1) with 11 individuals affected by auriculocondylar syndrome and confirmed variable features within the family. Facial asymmetry was highly prevalent among the patients. The authors noted that this feature had not been highlighted in earlier ACS reports. ACS is characterized by malformed 'question mark' ears, prominent cheeks, microstomia, an abnormal temporomandibular joint and mandibular condyle hypoplasia.

subject: Masotti et al. (2008)
object: Masotti et al. (2008) performed linkage analysis in two large ACS families, F1 and F2. Segregation analysis excluded the Treacher Collins syndrome, oculoauriculovertebral spectrum and Townes-Brocks syndrome loci. A genomewide search then found evidence of linkage to 1p21.1-q23.3 in family F2 (maximum lod score 3.01 at theta = 0), which defined the first ACS locus (ACS1).

subject: Masotti et al. (2008)
object: Masotti et al. (2008) found that the 1p21.1-q23.3 locus linked in family F2 was not linked to the phenotype segregating in family F1. They concluded that ACS is genetically heterogeneous, with at least two loci responsible for the phenotype.

subject: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022)
object: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) studied a previously reported non-consanguineous four-generation Brazilian family with 11 members showing typical features of auriculocondylar syndrome. Of the 10 documented, most had question mark ears (8 of 10), microstomia (8 of 10), and micrognathia (6 of 10), with considerable intrafamilial variability. The patients did not have large, open fontanelles, the hallmark of trisomy 7p.

subject: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022)
object: In the Brazilian ARCND family, in which Sanger sequencing of PLCB4, GNAI3, and EDN1 revealed no pathogenic variants, Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) performed genomewide SNP linkage analysis (9 affected, 3 unaffected genotyped) under an autosomal dominant model and found a maximum LOD score of 2.88 (maximum theoretical 2.93) in a 17.6-Mb region on chromosome 7 (chr7:14,395,902-32,017,194, hg38), narrowed by microsatellite markers to chr7:14,395,902-28,158,440. Gene prioritization ranked TWIST1 as the top candidate in the region.

subject: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022)
object: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) found no causative variants by whole-exome sequencing in 4 affected family members (a synonymous TRIL variant did not segregate). Targeted resequencing of a 2.4-Mb region around TWIST1 identified a 430,302-bp tandem duplication (NC_000007.14:g.18437239_18867540dup) beginning about 280 kb telomeric to TWIST1 and covering most of HDAC9; breakpoint PCR and Sanger sequencing showed segregation with the phenotype, with all unaffected individuals negative, suggesting full penetrance. Full-length catalytically active HDAC9 isoforms were predicted to be disrupted.

subject: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022)
object: Capture-C analysis in human embryonic calvarial mesenchymal cells, using the TWIST1 promoter as viewpoint, by Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) showed multiple cis contacts, with the highest frequency telomeric of TWIST1 within HDAC9 and the duplicated region, implying that the region contains TWIST1 regulatory elements (including enhancer eTw6) and providing a possible pathogenic mechanism.

subject: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022)
object: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) noted 19 DECIPHER patients with copy-number gains in the region; 7 had ear malformations and 7 micrognathia, mostly with larger duplications including the TWIST1 enhancer eTW6. One 179-kb duplication (276644) lying entirely within the ARCND duplicated region but not spanning the TWIST1 regulatory elements was not associated with ARCND features.

subject: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022)
object: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) generated iPSCs from 3 affected family members and controls and differentiated them into neural crest cells (iNCCs) and mesenchymal stem-like cells (nMSCs). Patient iNCCs showed increased HDAC9 (3.15-fold) and TWIST1 (2.03-fold) mRNA and a 4.3-fold decrease in migratory capacity, with no cell-cycle difference. Patient nMSCs showed reduced ALP activity (20.3-fold decrease) and expression and subtly reduced matrix mineralization, indicating delayed or impaired osteogenic differentiation; the authors suggested that TWIST1 deregulation contributes to ARCND via compromised neural crest migration and osteogenesis.
